query.original_query: syntactic complexity of LLM generated text and reasoning quality self-generated language structure

sub_queries.semantic_query: syntactic complexity and reasoning quality in LLM generated text, self-generated language structure, internal representations of syntax and reasoning, circuit analysis of language generation
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the relationship between syntactic complexity and reasoning quality in language model outputs by analyzing internal circuit mechanisms. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize knowledge representations within the residual stream that correlate with the generation of complex syntactic structures, such as nested clauses and long-range dependencies. Our analysis reveals that specific attention heads in middle and late layers are causally implicated in maintaining syntactic coherence during multi-step reasoning tasks. We find that when these heads are ablated, generated text exhibits reduced syntactic complexity and a corresponding degradation in logical consistency and stepwise argumentation. Further, we examine self-generated language structure by comparing internal feature activations during reasoning versus free-form generation. Results show that the same MLP layers and attention circuits are differentially recruited when the model must track hierarchical syntactic dependencies while performing deductive inference. This suggests that syntactic scaffolding is not merely a stylistic artifact but is functionally integrated with the model’s reasoning circuits. Our findings contribute to understanding how linguistic form and logical content are jointly encoded in transformer representations.

sub_queries.semantic_query: syntactic complexity in human language production and reasoning, self-generated language structure, relationship between syntactic complexity and reasoning quality
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the relationship between syntactic complexity in self-generated language and the quality of subsequent reasoning. Participants completed a verbal reasoning task requiring them to articulate solutions aloud. We measured syntactic complexity using established metrics, including mean length of utterance, clause density, and the proportion of embedded relative clauses in the elicited speech samples. Reasoning quality was independently rated on a scale of logical coherence and depth of argumentation. Results indicate a significant positive correlation between higher clause density and superior reasoning scores, even after controlling for total utterance length. Findings support the hypothesis that the online generation of more syntactically complex structures reflects a greater cognitive capacity for integrating multiple propositions, which facilitates more coherent reasoning. This pattern aligns with predictions from the capacity theory of sentence production, suggesting that syntactic planning demands share resources with higher-order executive functions involved in logical argument construction.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: A Modular Dataset to Demonstrate LLM Abstraction Capability
papers.research_question: Do LLMs have an internal representation of reasoning correctness and abstraction in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally encode representations of reasoning correctness, with strongest signals in middle-late layers, and they distinguish between logical and semantic equivalence in abstract reasoning concepts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess internal representations of reasoning correctness and abstraction, which can inform future efforts to enhance model reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
A classifier trained on LLM activations achieves over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning step correctness.
LLMs have internal representations of reasoning correctness, strongest in middle-late Transformer layers.
LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts that separate logical from semantic equivalence.
Abstraction level varies across layers, with middle layers containing more abstract information.
The reasoning representations are similar across top-performing layers, suggesting redundant encoding.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to structured logic puzzles, may not generalize to real-world scenarios.
Classifier's success may not generalize to other types of reasoning problems.
Reliance on probing techniques does not provide mechanistic explanation of how representations emerge.
Classifier trained on single LLM architecture, generalizability across models unclear.
future_direction: Explore more diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Conduct broader cross-model analyses including LRM models.
Develop methods for directly steering LLM reasoning based on learned representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but struggle with reasoning errors due to hallucinations and flawed logic. To investigate their internal representations of reasoning, we introduce ArrangementPuzzle, a novel puzzle dataset with structured solutions and automated stepwise correctness verification. We trained a classifier model on LLM activations on this dataset and found that it achieved over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning correctness, implying that LLMs internally distinguish between correct and incorrect reasoning steps, with the strongest representations in middle-late Transformer layers. Further analysis reveals that LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts within the middle activation layers of the transformer architecture, distinguishing logical from semantic equivalence. These findings provide insights into LLM reasoning mechanisms and contribute to improving AI reliability and interpretability, thereby offering the possibility to manipulate and refine LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: From Chains to DAGs: Probing the Graph Structure of Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of LLMs encode graph-structured reasoning (as directed acyclic graphs) beyond linear chains, and where does this structure emerge across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework to test whether LLM hidden states linearly encode reasoning DAG structure, and finds that such structure is meaningfully encoded, peaking in intermediate layers, and varies with node depth, edge span, and model scale.
papers.conclusion: LLM reasoning is not purely sequential, but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.
papers.key_findings:
DAG structure is meaningfully encoded in LLM representations.
Recoverability of DAG structure peaks in intermediate layers.
Recovery varies systematically by node depth, edge span, and model scale.
The framework enables nontrivial recovery of dependency graphs.
Larger models achieve higher recoverability, and reasoning-oriented training recipes provide modest gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on frozen pretrained models; it remains open whether fine-tuning or reinforcement learning alters the internal geometry of reasoning.
The probing approach assumes that reasoning DAG structure is linearly accessible in hidden states; nonlinear or distributed encodings may require more expressive probes.
The DAG formalization for GSM8K relies on GPT-5 mini, which may introduce noise or bias.
future_direction: Extend the framework to dynamic or cyclic reasoning.
Incorporate more expressive probes.
Investigate how training interventions affect internal reasoning structure.
papers.abstract: Recent progress in large language models has renewed interest in mechanistically characterizing how multi-step reasoning is represented and computed. While much prior work treats reasoning as a linear chain of steps, many reasoning problems are more naturally structured as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where intermediate conclusions may depend on multiple premises, branch into parallel sub-derivations, and later merge or be reused. Understanding whether such graph-structured reasoning is reflected in model internals remains an open question. In this work, we introduce Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework that directly asks whether LLM hidden states encode the geometry of a reasoning DAG in a linearly accessible form, and where this structure emerges across layers. Within this framework, we associate each reasoning node with a textual realization and train lightweight probes to predict two graph-theoretic properties from hidden states: node depth and pairwise node distance. We use these probes to analyze the layerwise emergence of DAG structure and evaluate controls that disrupt reasoning-relevant structure while preserving superficial textual properties. Our results provide evidence that reasoning DAG geometry is meaningfully encoded in intermediate layers, with recoverability varying systematically by node depth and model scale, suggesting that LLM reasoning is not only sequential but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: That Looks Hard: Characterizing Linguistic Complexity in Humans and Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the relationship between online (eye-tracking) and offline (human judgment) measures of sentence complexity and how they are modeled in a neural language model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of linguistic phenomena correlated with eye-tracking and human complexity judgments, compares feature-based and neural models for predicting complexity, and shows that fine-tuning a language model on complexity tasks leads to increased encoding of relevant linguistic properties in its representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a connection between eye-tracking metrics and explicit complexity perception, shows comparable performance between feature-based and neural models, and finds that fine-tuning on complexity tasks leads to the natural emergence of task-related linguistic properties in the model's representations, suggesting a link between acquired linguistic knowledge and downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence length is the most correlated predictor for all complexity metrics, but other linguistic features also contribute.
When controlling for sentence length, online and offline complexity metrics show different correlations with linguistic features.
ALBERT performs on par with an SVM using explicit linguistic features for predicting complexity, suggesting it implicitly learns relevant linguistic properties.
Probing experiments show that fine-tuning on complexity tasks increases the model's encoding of complexity-related linguistic features in its representations.
The model's linguistic competencies acquired during training are interpretable and related to its predictive performance on complexity tasks.
papers.limitation:
The fine-tuning corpora are small in size.
The SVM model with explicit features performs poorly on larger length bins, likely due to limited data affecting generalization.
future_direction: Test the effectiveness of tasks inspired by human language learning as intermediate steps to train more robust and parsimonious neural language models.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between two complementary perspectives in the human assessment of sentence complexity and how they are modeled in a neural language model (NLM). The first perspective takes into account multiple online behavioral metrics obtained from eye-tracking recordings. The second one concerns the offline perception of complexity measured by explicit human judgments. Using a broad spectrum of linguistic features modeling lexical, morpho-syntactic, and syntactic properties of sentences, we perform a comprehensive analysis of linguistic phenomena associated with the two complexity viewpoints and report similarities and differences. We then show the effectiveness of linguistic features when explicitly leveraged by a regression model for predicting sentence complexity and compare its results with the ones obtained by a fine-tuned neural language model. We finally probe the NLM's linguistic competence before and after fine-tuning, highlighting how linguistic information encoded in representations changes when the model learns to predict complexity.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Parrot Mind: Towards Explaining the Complex Task Reasoning of Pretrained Large Language Models with Template-Content Structure
papers.research_question: How can pretrained large language models learn to solve complex reasoning tasks with limited training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the template-content structure (T-C structure) as an intrinsic constraint in language that reduces the learning space from exponential to linear, explaining how LLMs can generalize on complex reasoning tasks with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The template-content structure provides a plausible explanation for how LLMs acquire complex reasoning abilities through language modeling, and empirical evidence supports its existence in current models.
papers.key_findings:
The T-C structure exists in current LLMs, as evidenced by lower variance in template token outputs compared to content tokens.
The T-C structure reduces the hypothesis space from exponential to linear, enabling within-task generalization.
Hierarchical T-C structure further reduces the space to logarithmic, enabling task composition across sub-tasks.
Larger models exhibit clearer T-C structure, with higher AUC in classifying template vs. content tokens.
The T-C structure explains how LLMs can perform reasoning through language modeling (parroting) by learning and reusing templates.
papers.limitation:
The T-C structure may not hold for all tasks, such as purely natural language tasks like translation or chatting.
The assumption of token-wise alignment is a simplification; semantic alignment is more realistic but introduces challenges.
The framework assumes deterministic generation, while practical models output probability distributions and use sampling.
future_direction: Extending the framework to handle sampling and probability distributions.
Investigating the disentanglement of semantic and position information in Transformers.
Applying the T-C structure to more complex tasks and real-world scenarios.
papers.abstract: The pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have shown their extraordinary capacity to solve reasoning tasks, even on tasks that require a complex process involving multiple sub-steps. However, given the vast possible generation space of all the tasks, how the pretrained model learns the reasoning ability remains an open question. We firstly propose that an intrinsic structural constraint on the generated sequence of language-based reasoning -- we called it template-content structure (T-C structure) -- is the key to explain why LLMs can solve a large number of complex reasoning problems with limited training data by showing this structure can reduce the possible space from exponential level to linear level. Furthermore, by generalizing this structure to the hierarchical case, we demonstrate that models can achieve task composition, further reducing the space needed to learn from linear to logarithmic, thereby effectively learning on complex reasoning involving multiple steps. We provide both examples and formal theory of our T-C structure. We also experimentally validate the existence of the T-C structure in some current LLMs and its effectiveness for reasoning.

papers.title: Understanding Syntax in Large Language Models: Successes and Limitations
papers.research_question: How accurately can LLMs handle published examples of complex syntactic phenomena, as described in linguistic theories?
papers.core_contribution: This study evaluates the syntactic competence of LLMs, finding that while they handle simple constructions well, they struggle with complex hierarchical dependencies, highlighting the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles.
papers.conclusion: LLMs demonstrate competence in simple syntax but struggle with complex structures, indicating a gap between surface fluency and deep syntactic competence, necessitating hybrid approaches for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit high success rates for simple relative clauses and basic wh-movement, but performance declines with increased complexity.
Center-embedding poses significant challenges, with success rates dropping to around 50% for deeply embedded structures.
Errors include truncation of sentences, unresolved syntactic dependencies, and semantic incoherence in complex cases.
LLMs rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than deep generative syntactic principles.
The limitations suggest that current LLMs lack robust internal representations of hierarchical syntax.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relied exclusively on examples from English linguistic literature, not capturing syntactic diversity across languages.
The evaluation focused only on relative clauses, wh-movement, and center-embedding, without exploring broader syntactic constructs.
The study was limited to publicly available LLMs like GPT-4 and BERT, without considering effects of model size, architecture, or training data.
The evaluation did not delve into underlying representations or mechanisms of the models.
future_direction: Integrating explicit syntactic theory into neural architectures, such as the Minimalist Program or dependency grammar.
Conducting cross-linguistic comparisons to evaluate LLMs' syntactic competence across different languages.
Designing more linguistically focused benchmarks based on theoretical constructs like syntactic islands or scope ambiguity.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to process complex syntactic phenomena, including relative clauses, wh-movement, and center- embedding. By analyzing examples derived from linguistic literature, the study highlights both the strengths and limitations of LLMs in handling syntax. The results reveal that while LLMs exhibit competence in simpler syntactic constructions, they struggle with deeper hierarchical dependencies and abstract syntactic constraints. The study underscores the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles into LLM architectures to bridge the gap between surface-level fluency and generative linguistic competence.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Should Neural Network Architecture Reflect Linguistic Structure?
papers.research_question: Should neural network architecture reflect linguistic structure for better language modeling and representation of sentence meanings?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces recurrent neural network grammars (RNNGs) that incorporate hierarchical syntactic structure, showing they outperform sequential and tree-structured RNNs in language generation and downstream semantic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Neural network architectures that reflect linguistic structure, such as RNNGs, are more effective for language modeling and representation.
papers.key_findings:
RNNGs achieve better language generation results compared to models that do not exploit linguistic structure.
Unsupervised learning of syntactic structures using reinforcement learning improves performance on downstream semantic tasks over sequential and tree-structured RNNs.
papers.abstract: I explore the hypothesis that conventional neural network models (e.g., recurrent neural networks) are incorrectly biased for making linguistically sensible generalizations when learning, and that a better class of models is based on architectures that reflect hierarchical structures for which considerable behavioral evidence exists. I focus on the problem of modeling and representing the meanings of sentences. On the generation front, I introduce recurrent neural network grammars (RNNGs), a joint, generative model of phrase-structure trees and sentences. RNNGs operate via a recursive syntactic process reminiscent of probabilistic context-free grammar generation, but decisions are parameterized using RNNs that condition on the entire (top-down, left-to-right) syntactic derivation history, thus relaxing context-free independence assumptions, while retaining a bias toward explaining decisions via "syntactically local" conditioning contexts. Experiments show that RNNGs obtain better results in generating language than models that don't exploit linguistic structure. On the representation front, I explore unsupervised learning of syntactic structures based on distant semantic supervision using a reinforcement-learning algorithm. The learner seeks a syntactic structure that provides a compositional architecture that produces a good representation for a downstream semantic task. Although the inferred structures are quite different from traditional syntactic analyses, the performance on the downstream tasks surpasses that of systems that use sequential RNNs and tree-structured RNNs based on treebank dependencies.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms support abstract reasoning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an emergent three-stage symbolic architecture in LLMs that implements abstract reasoning via symbol abstraction heads, symbolic induction heads, and retrieval heads.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform abstract reasoning via emergent symbolic mechanisms, suggesting a resolution to the debate between symbolic and neural network approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Symbol abstraction heads in early layers convert input tokens to abstract variables based on relations.
Symbolic induction heads in intermediate layers perform sequence induction over abstract variables.
Retrieval heads in later layers retrieve the token associated with the predicted abstract variable.
These mechanisms are robust across multiple abstract reasoning tasks and model families.
Representations in these heads encode abstract variables invariant to specific tokens, and better representation correlates with correct performance.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have found evidence for emergent reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), but debate persists concerning the robustness of these capabilities, and the extent to which they depend on structured reasoning mechanisms. To shed light on these issues, we study the internal mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in LLMs. We identify an emergent symbolic architecture that implements abstract reasoning via a series of three computations. In early layers, symbol abstraction heads convert input tokens to abstract variables based on the relations between those tokens. In intermediate layers, symbolic induction heads perform sequence induction over these abstract variables. Finally, in later layers, retrieval heads predict the next token by retrieving the value associated with the predicted abstract variable. These results point toward a resolution of the longstanding debate between symbolic and neural network approaches, suggesting that emergent reasoning in neural networks depends on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Mechanisms vs. Outcomes: Probing for Syntax Fails to Explain Performance on Targeted Syntactic Evaluations
papers.research_question: Do probing accuracies, measured by dependency tree attachment scores of syntactic probes, effectively predict a model’s downstream performance on targeted syntactic evaluations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations, highlighting a disconnect between latent syntactic representations and observable syntactic behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Probing fails to reliably extract the latent syntactic knowledge within models that correlates with minimal pair accuracy, arguing for targeted evaluations like BLiMP as the gold standard for assessing syntactic competence.
papers.key_findings:
No significant regression fit between probing accuracy and overall BLiMP minimal pair accuracy across 32 models.
Only anaphor agreement shows a significant correlation, but a non-syntactic control probe yields a similar fit, suggesting it is spurious.
Probe recovery of critical syntactic edges (e.g., subject-verb) only weakly aligns with minimal pair outcomes (40–60% match rate).
In over 85% of BLiMP paradigms, UUAS score distributions for correct and incorrect minimal pairs substantially overlap.
Control probes trained on non-syntactic information can also predict some syntactic benchmark performance, indicating that probing results may not be attributable solely to syntactic representations.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation only uses English grammatical benchmarks.
Probe architectures are limited to linear and bilinear probes; other architectures could yield different results.
Models are limited to up to 8B parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Extending the work to multilingual benchmarks (e.g., MultiBLiMP, TurBLiMP).
Exploring other probe architectures and syntactic probing tasks.
Investigating causal relationships between probed representations and model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a robust mastery of syntax when processing and generating text. While this suggests internalized understanding of hierarchical syntax and dependency relations, the precise mechanism by which they represent syntactic structure is an open area within interpretability research. Probing provides one way to identify the mechanism of syntax being linearly encoded in activations, however, no comprehensive study has yet established whether a model's probing accuracy reliably predicts its downstream syntactic performance. Adopting a "mechanisms vs. outcomes" framework, we evaluate 32 open-weight transformer models and find that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations across English linguistic phenomena. Our results highlight a substantial disconnect between latent syntactic representations found via probing and observable syntactic behaviors in downstream tasks.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally perform a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements a backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree one level per layer, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a certain depth, using parallelized strategies and heuristics, which provides insights into the operating principles of transformers for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head concatenates edge tokens by copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers perform backward chaining, moving one step up the tree per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining from multiple subgoals and merges subpaths.
The model uses a one-step lookahead heuristic to identify child nodes and avoid leaf nodes when backward chaining is insufficient.
The model's reasoning is depth-bounded and resorts to heuristics beyond its depth limit.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a synthetic symbolic reasoning task and may not directly translate to natural language tasks.
The input format uses shuffled edge lists in backward order, and the mechanisms might vary for other arrangements.
papers.abstract: Transformers demonstrate impressive performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks. To evaluate the degree to which these abilities are a result of actual reasoning, existing work has focused on developing sophisticated benchmarks for behavioral studies. However, these studies do not provide insights into the internal mechanisms driving the observed capabilities. To improve our understanding of the internal mechanisms of transformers, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of a transformer trained on a synthetic reasoning task. We identify a set of interpretable mechanisms the model uses to solve the task, and validate our findings using correlational and causal evidence. Our results suggest that it implements a depth-bounded recurrent mechanisms that operates in parallel and stores intermediate results in selected token positions. We anticipate that the motifs we identified in our synthetic setting can provide valuable insights into the broader operating principles of transformers and thus provide a basis for understanding more complex models.

papers.title: The Grammar of Transformers: A Systematic Review of Interpretability Research on Syntactic Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What do Transformer-based language models (TLMs) learn about syntax from the language modeling task?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic review of 337 articles on syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models, identifying an over-focus on English and BERT, and finding that TLMs capture form-oriented syntactic phenomena well but perform more variably on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface.
papers.conclusion: The review reveals a rich but heterogeneous landscape in syntactic interpretability research, with tentative evidence that formal syntax is easier for models than the syntax-semantics interface, and highlights the need for broader empirical scope and better data reporting.
papers.key_findings:
