papers.research_question: When do language models use syntactic information causally? How can we design probes to avoid false negatives due to redundant encodings of syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dropout probes, a new neural probing architecture that encourages probes to use all relevant representations of syntax in model embeddings, enabling better causal analysis and performance improvement via syntactic information injection.
papers.conclusion: Dropout probes are effective for causal analysis of language models and can be used to improve model performance by injecting syntactic information, but further work is needed to extend the approach.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode syntactic information redundantly in their embeddings.
Dropout probes reveal causal use of syntactic representations in QA models where prior methods did not.
Injecting syntactic information at test time can improve QA model performance on syntactically challenging tasks.
NLI models do not show causal use of syntax even with dropout probes.
Dropout probes can boost model performance without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Systematic evaluation of models for many layers, multiple probes, and many counterfactuals is computationally challenging.
The transparency benefits require access to the internals of the pretrained model.
The technique is limited to diagnosis of existing models and does not train models to respond appropriately to interventions.
future_direction: Studying pretrained models beyond those considered in this work.
Further research into redundancy in embeddings.
More investigation into inserting symbolic knowledge into neural representations.
New methods for training models to respond appropriately to interventions.
papers.abstract: Recent causal probing literature reveals when language models and syntactic probes use similar representations. Such techniques may yield "false negative" causality results: models may use representations of syntax, but probes may have learned to use redundant encodings of the same syntactic information. We demonstrate that models do encode syntactic information redundantly and introduce a new probe design that guides probes to consider all syntactic information present in embeddings. Using these probes, we find evidence for the use of syntax in models where prior methods did not, allowing us to boost model performance by injecting syntactic information into representations.

papers.title: ReJump: A Tree-Jump Representation for Analyzing and Improving LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we represent an LLM’s reasoning trace to facilitate a comprehensive analysis and comparison of its internal behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ReJump, a tree-jump representation for LLM reasoning traces, enabling comprehensive analysis and comparison of reasoning behaviors, and demonstrates its utility for improving reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: ReJump provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing and comparing LLM reasoning behaviors, and can be leveraged to improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Models with similar final accuracy can exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors.
Different tasks favor different reasoning styles (e.g., varying balance between exploration and exploitation).
LRMs exhibit more deliberate reasoning behaviors (e.g., exploration and verification) compared to CoT-prompted LLMs.
Distilled models inherit reasoning behaviors from their teachers.
ReJump can improve reasoning quality at test time through strategies such as ReJump-guided Best-of-N selection and prompt selection.
papers.limitation: Tree and jump similarity metrics only capture logical structure and action-transition distributions, overlooking semantic content and temporal patterns.
future_direction: Incorporating semantic information and temporal dynamics into the ReJump representation and metrics.
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are Large Language Models (LLMs) explicitly trained to generate long-form Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs), achieving impressive success on challenging tasks like math and programming. However, their underlying reasoning "algorithms" remain poorly understood. To investigate this, we propose ReJump, which represents a reasoning trace as a visitation order over nodes in a tree of intermediate problem-solving steps. Transitions between nodes, which we term jumps, include adjacent moves that capture behaviors such as calculation, and non-adjacent moves that capture behaviors such as backtracking and verification. ReJump enables analyzing LLM reasoning with diverse metrics that quantify exploration, exploitation, overthinking, forgetting, and verification. Using our proposed LLM agent to extract reasoning traces into ReJump format, we evaluate state-of-the-art LRMs on two tasks and find that models with similar accuracy can exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors, while different tasks favor different reasoning styles (e.g., varying balance between exploration and exploitation). To further understand how learning strategies shape reasoning, we use ReJump to compare distilled LRMs with their teachers, CoT-prompted LLMs with LRMs, and to examine how the number of reasoning examples and reinforcement learning affect reasoning behavior. Finally, we show that ReJump can improve reasoning quality at test time through strategies such as ReJump-guided Best-of-N selection and prompt selection. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/UW-Madison-Lee-Lab/ReJump.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong generalization across a wide range of tasks. Reasoning with LLMs is central to solving multi-step problems and complex decision-making. To support efficient reasoning, recent studies have shifted attention from explicit chain-of-thought prompting toward implicit reasoning, where reasoning occurs silently via latent structures without emitting intermediate textual steps. Implicit reasoning brings advantages such as lower generation cost, faster inference, and better alignment with internal computation. Although prior surveys have discussed latent representations in the context of reasoning, a dedicated and mechanism-level examination of how reasoning unfolds internally within LLMs remains absent. This survey fills that gap by introducing a taxonomy centered on execution paradigms, shifting the focus from representational forms to computational strategies. We organize existing methods into three execution paradigms based on \textbf{\textit{how and where internal computation unfolds}}: latent optimization, signal-guided control, and layer-recurrent execution. We also review structural, behavioral and representation-based evidence that supports the presence of implicit reasoning in LLMs. We further provide a structured overview of the evaluation metrics and benchmarks used in existing works to assess the effectiveness and reliability of implicit reasoning. We maintain a continuously updated project at: https://github.com/digailab/awesome-llm-implicit-reasoning.

papers.title: Do Neural Language Models Show Preferences for Syntactic Formalisms?
papers.research_question: When probing language models for syntactic dependency structure, is Universal Dependencies (UD) the best fit, or is the representational structure better explained by Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD)? Are these patterns consistent across typologically different languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that neural language models (BERT and ELMo) encode syntactic structure that aligns better with the deep-syntactic style of Universal Dependencies (UD) than the surface-oriented Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD), and this preference is consistent across most languages and correlated with tree height differences.
papers.conclusion: The syntactic structure captured by neural language models aligns better with UD than SUD, and this alignment is influenced by linguistic factors and tree shape, with UD being a better fit for most languages.
papers.key_findings:
Both BERT and ELMo exhibit a preference for UD over SUD in most languages.
The preference for UD is stronger in languages with a high proportion of function words (like adpositions) and where SUD trees are significantly higher.
In agglutinative languages (Basque, Finnish, Turkish) the preference is less clear or even reversed.
The difference in tree height between UD and SUD is strongly correlated with the probing accuracy difference.
The probe performs best when combining information from multiple layers (weighted average).
papers.limitation: The probe combines two separate probes (distance and depth) and is not optimized for UAS directly, which may affect the validity of the extracted trees.
future_direction: Exploring probes that combine the distance and depth assumptions into a single transformation.
Methods for alleviating treebank supervision altogether.
Revisiting the insights within a non-probing framework, such as Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.abstract: Recent work on the interpretability of deep neural language models has concluded that many properties of natural language syntax are encoded in their representational spaces. However, such studies often suffer from limited scope by focusing on a single language and a single linguistic formalism. In this study, we aim to investigate the extent to which the semblance of syntactic structure captured by language models adheres to a surface-syntactic or deep syntactic style of analysis, and whether the patterns are consistent across different languages. We apply a probe for extracting directed dependency trees to BERT and ELMo models trained on 13 different languages, probing for two different syntactic annotation styles: Universal Dependencies (UD), prioritizing deep syntactic relations, and Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD), focusing on surface structure. We find that both models exhibit a preference for UD over SUD -with interesting variations across languages and layers -and that the strength of this preference is correlated with differences in tree shape.

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding of Language Models in Syntactic Code Completion
papers.research_question: How does CodeLlama-7b perform the syntactic code completion task of closing parentheses? Specifically, at which layers does the model realize the correct token, how do layers and sub-layers contribute, and how do attention heads function in this task?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic interpretability study of CodeLlama-7b on a syntactic code completion task (closing parentheses), revealing that the model uses middle-to-late layers with MHA being particularly crucial, and identifies attention heads that track closed parentheses but may promote incorrect knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides preliminary insights into how Code LMs use internal knowledge for syntax completion, identifying critical attention heads and suggesting future work on circuit discovery and universality.
papers.key_findings:
The model only realizes the correct token from middle-to-late layers, with the Two Closing Parentheses task being easier (earlier layers) than Three or Four.
Both MHA and FF sub-layers contribute to the task, but MHA sub-layers are more critical.
Attention heads L30H0 and L27H24 track the number of already closed parentheses, but L27H24 always promotes two closing parentheses (incorrect knowledge association), leading to negative effects when more are needed.
future_direction: Circuit discovery to include MLP sub-layers and portray a complete circuit.
Investigating universality of the interpretation across similar tasks and programming languages.
Improving LM performance by suppressing less precise attention heads.
papers.abstract: Recently, language models (LMs) have shown impressive proficiency in code generation tasks, especially when fine-tuned on code-specific datasets, commonly known as Code LMs. However, our understanding of the internal decision-making processes of Code LMs, such as how they use their (syntactic or semantic) knowledge, remains limited, which could lead to unintended harm as they are increasingly used in real life. This motivates us to conduct one of the first Mechanistic Interpretability works to understand how Code LMs perform a syntactic completion task, specifically the closing parenthesis task, on the CodeLlama-7b model (Roziere et al. 2023). Our findings reveal that the model requires middle-later layers until it can confidently predict the correct label for the closing parenthesis task. Additionally, we identify that while both multi-head attention (MHA) and feed-forward (FF) sub-layers play essential roles, MHA is particularly crucial. Furthermore, we also discover attention heads that keep track of the number of already closed parentheses precisely but may or may not promote a correct number of closing parentheses that are still missing, leading to a positive or negative impact on the model's performance.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: Language Model Behavior: A Comprehensive Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes over 250 recent studies on the behavior of pre-trained English Transformer language models, highlighting their capabilities in syntax, semantics, pragmatics, world knowledge, and reasoning, as well as weaknesses such as sensitivity to input variations, unfactual responses, and social biases.
papers.conclusion: Language models remain sensitive to specific inputs and surface features even as they scale to hundreds of billions of parameters. Many model strengths and weaknesses can be framed as correct or incorrect generalizations of text patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Language models possess basic capabilities in syntax, semantics, pragmatics, world knowledge, and reasoning, but these capabilities are sensitive to specific inputs and surface features.
Despite dramatic increases in generated text quality as models scale to hundreds of billions of parameters, the models are still prone to unfactual responses, commonsense errors, memorized text, and social biases.
Many of the weaknesses exhibited by large language models can be interpreted as examples of over-generalization or under-generalization of patterns learned from text.
Syntactic abilities are learned fairly robustly early in pre-training, but performance degrades in more complex or infrequent examples, such as subject-verb agreement with intervening clauses.
Language models' performance on reasoning and knowledge tasks is highly dependent on the specific input phrasing and context, reflecting a systematic under-generalization of patterns to novel contexts.
papers.limitation: The survey is limited to English language models and does not cover fine-tuned models or non-behavioral (mechanistic) analyses.
future_direction: Expanding to less well-studied languages for which language models often perform poorly.
Investigating the specific linguistic patterns and types of patterns that language models over-generalize and under-generalize.
Bridging the gap between behavioral and mechanistic levels of language model analysis.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have received widespread public attention, yet their generated text is often surprising even to NLP researchers. In this survey, we discuss over 250 recent studies of English language model behavior before task-specific fine-tuning. Language models possess basic capabilities in syntax, semantics, pragmatics, world knowledge, and reasoning, but these capabilities are sensitive to specific inputs and surface features. Despite dramatic increases in generated text quality as models scale to hundreds of billions of parameters, the models are still prone to unfactual responses, commonsense errors, memorized text, and social biases. Many of these weaknesses can be framed as over-generalizations or under-generalizations of learned patterns in text. We synthesize recent results to highlight what is currently known about large language model capabilities, thus providing a resource for applied work and for research in adjacent fields that use language models.

papers.title: REMA: A Unified Reasoning Manifold Framework for Interpreting Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we understand and localize reasoning failures in Large Language Models by analyzing the geometric structure of their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of the 'Reasoning Manifold' and the REMA framework, which diagnoses reasoning failures by quantifying and localizing the geometric deviation of erroneous internal representations from the manifold formed by correct ones.
papers.conclusion: REMA provides a novel geometric perspective for interpreting LLM reasoning, demonstrating that deviations from a 'Reasoning Manifold' are indicative of errors and allowing for the localization of failure points within the model's inference path.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states of both correct and incorrect reasoning exhibit low-dimensional structures (low Intrinsic Dimension).
Representations of erroneous reasoning consistently show statistically significant geometric deviation from the manifold of correct reasoning.
These deviations can be traced back to specific model layers (divergence points), revealing model- and task-dependent patterns of failure origins.
The relative deviation distance is negatively correlated with model accuracy, suggesting more difficult tasks lead to larger deviations.
Correct and error reasoning representations are highly separable in the latent space, as shown by UMAP/t-SNE visualizations and classifier accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The manifold approximation depends on the diversity and density of the correct samples.
Binary partitioning of samples into 'correct' and 'error' based on exact text match might misclassify 'nearly correct' reasoning.
future_direction: Building more precise manifold models using advanced manifold learning techniques.
Investigating the fundamental reasons for the formation of reasoning manifolds.
Exploring more fine-grained, confidence-based, or soft-scoring-based partitioning methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform complex reasoning and their failure mechanisms is a challenge in interpretability research. To provide a measurable geometric analysis perspective, we define the concept of the Reasoning Manifold, a latent low-dimensional geometric structure formed by the internal representations corresponding to all correctly reasoned generations. This structure can be conceptualized as the embodiment of the effective thinking paths that the model has learned to successfully solve a given task. Based on this concept, we build REMA, a framework that explains the origins of failures by quantitatively comparing the spatial relationships of internal model representations corresponding to both erroneous and correct reasoning samples. Specifically, REMA first quantifies the geometric deviation of each erroneous representation by calculating its k-nearest neighbors distance to the approximated manifold formed by correct representations, thereby providing a unified failure signal. It then localizes the divergence points where these deviations first become significant by tracking this deviation metric across the model's layers and comparing it against a baseline of internal fluctuations from correct representations, thus identifying where the reasoning chain begins to go off-track. Our extensive experiments on diverse language and multimodal models and tasks demonstrate the low-dimensional nature of the reasoning manifold and the high separability between erroneous and correct reasoning representations. The results also validate the effectiveness of the REMA framework in analyzing the origins of reasoning failures. This research connects abstract reasoning failures to measurable geometric deviations in representations, providing new avenues for in-depth understanding and diagnosis of the internal computational processes of black-box models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit differences in internal activations when processing prompts associated with different Bloom levels? At what depth do representations of cognitive complexity emerge? Is Bloom-level information linearly recoverable from hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probing shows that cognitive complexity levels (Bloom's Taxonomy) are linearly separable in the residual stream activations of LLMs, emerging early in the forward pass and becoming more separable across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a measurable, linearly separable internal representation of cognitive complexity that aligns closely with Bloom’s Taxonomy, validating it as a framework for auditing the internal mechanics of artificial cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Linear classifiers achieve ~95% mean accuracy in classifying Bloom levels from residual stream activations.
Cognitive complexity emerges early in the forward pass (around layer 5) and remains stable in deeper layers.
Misclassifications occur predominantly between adjacent Bloom levels, indicating that the representations preserve the ordinal structure of cognitive complexity.
Geometric analysis shows increasing centroid distances between adjacent Bloom levels across layers, indicating progressive disentanglement.
The findings are consistent across four different LLM architectures.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on decoder-only transformer architectures and English educational questions.
Generalizability to other architectures (e.g., encoder-only or encoder-decoder) and languages remains to be established.
Linear probes demonstrate linear accessibility but do not prove that the model uses this information causally during generation.
Methodology examines only the residual stream, leaving attention patterns and MLP internals as areas for future investigation.
future_direction: Causal intervention studies to validate whether the cognitive representations are functionally utilized by the model.
Cross-lingual and cross-domain analysis to establish universality of the findings.
Investigating attention patterns and MLP internals.
papers.abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of cognitive complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different cognitive levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve approximately 95% mean accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing strong evidence that cognitive level is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model resolves the cognitive difficulty of a prompt early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

papers.title: Three tiers of computation in transformers and in brain architectures
papers.research_question: What enabled transformer-based A.I. models to suddenly generate fluent natural language where previous AI models had failed, and why are current transformer-based models having difficulty obtaining arithmetic and logic skills?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark based on the grammar-automata hierarchy to evaluate computational capabilities, and provides a framework linking transitions in computational tiers to language and logic abilities in transformers and humans.
papers.conclusion: The grammar-automata hierarchy provides a principled framework for understanding the capabilities and limitations of transformers and humans, suggesting that architectural augmentations (like multiple memory stacks) are needed for logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs (under tens of billions of parameters) do not reliably process any of the formal grammar inputs.
Mid-sized LMs show some recognition of context-free grammar (CFG) but are unreliable on higher-level grammars.
Large LLMs and humans robustly recognize CFG and indexed grammar (IXG) strings, but not context-sensitive grammar (CSG) strings.
Interpolated Augmented LLMs (IALLMs) recognize CFG and IXG and also a significant portion (up to 44%) of CSG sentences.
The transition from single-stack to multi-stack memory in the automata hierarchy corresponds to the transition from language to logic abilities.
future_direction: Explore architectural changes to provide separate external memory stores to expand transformers to higher computational tiers.
Investigate the broader space of specific hybrid architectures, including interpolations of neurosymbolic methods.
papers.abstract: Human language and logic abilities are computationally quantified within the well-studied grammar-automata hierarchy. We identify three hierarchical tiers and two corresponding transitions and show their correspondence to specific abilities in transformer-based language models (LMs). These emergent abilities have often been described in terms of scaling; we show that it is the transition between tiers, rather than scaled size itself, that determines a system's capabilities. Specifically, humans effortlessly process language yet require critical training to perform arithmetic or logical reasoning tasks; and LMs possess language abilities absent from predecessor systems, yet still struggle with logical processing. We submit a novel benchmark of computational power, provide empirical evaluations of humans and fifteen LMs, and, most significantly, provide a theoretically grounded framework to promote careful thinking about these crucial topics. The resulting principled analyses provide explanatory accounts of the abilities and shortfalls of LMs, and suggest actionable insights into the expansion of their logic abilities.

papers.title: Transformers Pretrained on Procedural Data Contain Modular Structures for Algorithmic Reasoning
papers.research_question: What properties of pretraining data enable language models to acquire reasoning capabilities? Specifically, what is gained from procedural data, where does the useful knowledge reside in the pretrained models, and how does pretraining improve downstream capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining transformers on procedural data creates modular, transferable structures in different parts of the architecture (attention and MLP layers), which can be composed to jointly reinforce multiple algorithmic reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Procedural pretraining creates useful, modular structures in different parts of the transformer architecture, suggesting the possibility of disentangling the acquisition of knowledge from reasoning to improve model robustness and data efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Different forms of procedural data (e.g., k-DYCK, STACK, ECA) significantly improve specific downstream algorithmic reasoning capabilities (e.g., memory recall, arithmetic, sorting).
The beneficial inductive biases from pretraining often reside in specific architectural components, with attention layers being the most consistently transferable carrier of useful structure.
Pretraining creates soft inductive biases in precisely structured weights, not merely through adjusting weight magnitudes, as shown by sensitivity to noise and shuffling perturbations.
The structures induced by multiple pretraining rules are modular and can be composed (e.g., combining attention from one model with MLPs from another) to create an initialization that facilitates fine-tuning on multiple tasks.
future_direction: Understanding why specific forms of procedural data help specific capabilities (e.g., why HAYSTACK benefits from k-DYCK but not its SHUFFLE variant).
Exploring data mixture optimization to balance multiple procedural rules for training generalist LLMs.
Characterizing the resulting structure in pretrained models to directly instantiate it in initial weights, avoiding wasteful expansion of simple rules into millions of training examples.
papers.abstract: Pretraining on large, semantically rich datasets is key for developing language models. Surprisingly, recent studies have shown that even synthetic data, generated procedurally through simple semantic-free algorithms, can yield some of the same benefits as natural language pretraining. It is unclear what specific capabilities such simple synthetic data instils in a model, where these capabilities reside in the architecture, and how they manifest within its weights. In this short paper, we identify several beneficial forms of procedural data, together with specific algorithmic reasoning skills that improve in small transformers. Our core finding is that different procedural rules instil distinct but complementary inductive structures in the model. With extensive ablations and partial-transfer experiments, we discover that these structures reside in different parts of the model. Attention layers often carry the most transferable information, but some pretraining rules impart useful structure to MLP blocks instead. Most interestingly, the structures induced by multiple rules can be composed to jointly reinforce multiple capabilities. These results suggest an exciting possibility of disentangling the acquisition of knowledge from reasoning in language models, with the goal of improving their robustness and data efficiency.

papers.title: Logical Phase Transitions: Understanding Collapse in LLM Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does logical reasoning performance in LLMs change with increasing logical complexity? Does it degrade smoothly or collapse abruptly at critical thresholds?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Logical Complexity Metric (LoCM) and discovers Logical Phase Transitions (LPTs) in LLM reasoning, then proposes Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning to mitigate reasoning collapse at high logical complexity.
papers.conclusion: Logical Phase Transitions are a fundamental phenomenon in LLM reasoning, and Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning effectively mitigates reasoning collapse, improving performance and generalization across logical complexity levels.
papers.key_findings:
Logical reasoning performance in LLMs collapses abruptly beyond critical complexity thresholds, termed Logical Phase Transitions.
The proposed Logical Complexity Metric (LoCM) quantifies logical difficulty and reveals phase transitions.
Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning, which aligns natural language and symbolic representations and uses complexity-aware curriculum, mitigates reasoning collapse and improves generalization.
The method achieves average accuracy gains of +1.26 in naive prompting and +3.95 in CoT across five benchmarks.
Phase transitions are universal across open- and closed-source LLMs.
future_direction: Complexity-aware curriculum learning for reinforcement learning.
Process-level supervision via verifiable symbolic reasoning chains.
LoCM as a diagnostic tool for reasoning robustness.
papers.abstract: Symbolic logical reasoning is a critical yet underexplored capability of large language models (LLMs), providing reliable and verifiable decision-making in high-stakes domains such as mathematical reasoning and legal judgment. In this study, we present a systematic analysis of logical reasoning under controlled increases in logical complexity, and reveal a previously unrecognized phenomenon, which we term Logical Phase Transitions: rather than degrading smoothly, logical reasoning performance remains stable within a regime but collapses abruptly beyond a critical logical depth, mirroring physical phase transitions such as water freezing beyond a critical temperature threshold. Building on this insight, we propose Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning, a principled framework that adaptively aligns natural language with logical symbols to establish a shared representation, and reshapes training dynamics around phase-transition boundaries to progressively strengthen reasoning at increasing logical depths. Experiments on five benchmarks show that our approach effectively mitigates logical reasoning collapse at high complexity, yielding average accuracy gains of +1.26 in naive prompting and +3.95 in CoT, while improving generalization to unseen logical compositions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AI4SS/Logical-Phase-Transitions.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Controllable Text Generation with Language Constraints
papers.research_question: How can we control text generation in language models with constraints specified in natural language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a new benchmark (COGNAC) for controllable text generation with natural language constraints and proposes a method (COGNACGEN) that leverages a language model's internal knowledge to guide generation.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a new task and benchmark for controllable generation with natural language constraints, shows that even state-of-the-art models like GPT-3 fail often, and proposes COGNACGEN which improves performance by using the model's internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
COGNACGEN outperforms baselines like fine-tuning and self-debiasing in instruction conformance.
COGNACGEN with textual example guidance works best among the proposed guidance types.
COGNACGEN achieves higher instruction conformance than GPT-3 (davinci) despite having fewer parameters.
The trie-based decoding is effective for handling multi-token guidance.
Performance varies across categories and instruction templates, indicating room for improvement.
papers.limitation: The benchmark is limited by the comprehensiveness of the underlying knowledge bases (WordNet and Wikidata), which may not cover all relevant entities and could amplify existing biases.
papers.abstract: We consider the task of text generation in language models with constraints specified in natural language. To this end, we first create a challenging benchmark Cognac that provides as input to the model a topic with example text, along with a constraint on text to be avoided. Unlike prior work, our benchmark contains knowledge-intensive constraints sourced from databases like Wordnet and Wikidata, which allows for straightforward evaluation while striking a balance between broad attribute-level and narrow lexical-level controls. We find that even state-of-the-art language models like GPT-3 fail often on this task, and propose a solution to leverage a language model's own internal knowledge to guide generation. Our method, called CognacGen, first queries the language model to generate guidance terms for a specified topic or constraint, and uses the guidance to modify the model's token generation probabilities. We propose three forms of guidance (binary verifier, top-k tokens, textual example), and employ prefix-tuning approaches to distill the guidance to tackle diverse natural language constraints. Through extensive empirical evaluations, we demonstrate that CognacGen can successfully generalize to unseen instructions and outperform competitive baselines in generating constraint conforming text.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: Comprehension Without Competence: Architectural Limits of LLMs in Symbolic Computation and Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency, despite being able to fluently explain the correct principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes a fundamental architectural limitation in LLMs termed the 'computational split-brain syndrome,' where models can explain principles they cannot reliably execute, due to geometric separation of instruction and execution pathways.
papers.conclusion: LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning, and fundamental architectural innovations are needed to overcome these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a systematic gap between comprehension (explaining principles) and competence (executing them), termed computational split-brain syndrome.
This gap is rooted in architectural constraints: token embeddings resist domain binding, FFNs cannot implement exact symbolic operations, and next-token prediction decouples instruction from execution.
The syndrome manifests across domains (arithmetic and relational reasoning) and is not resolved by scaling or prompting.
Compensatory strategies (self-scaffolding, tool delegation, hybrid architectures) are necessary but highlight the need for metacognitive capabilities that current architectures lack.
Mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles.
papers.limitation:
Focus on pretrained transformer-based LLMs without external tools or explicit reasoning scaffolds.
Empirical evaluation centers on specific model families (LLaMA2, Claude, GPT-4) and may not generalize to fundamentally different architectures.
Geometric separation experiments rely on t-SNE projections which may not capture all relevant representational structure.
Theoretical analysis of FFN computational limits focuses on ReLU networks and may not apply to other activation functions.
future_direction: Developing future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution.
Empirical validation of the hypothesis that similar constraints apply to architectural variations like mixture-of-experts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) display striking surface fluency yet systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency. This paper offers a structural diagnosis of such failures, revealing a persistent gap between \textit{comprehension} and \textit{competence}. Through controlled experiments and architectural analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs often articulate correct principles without reliably applying them--a failure rooted not in knowledge access, but in computational execution. We term this phenomenon the computational \textit{split-brain syndrome}, where instruction and action pathways are geometrically and functionally dissociated. This core limitation recurs across domains, from mathematical operations to relational inferences, and explains why model behavior remains brittle even under idealized prompting. We argue that LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines, but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning. Our findings delineate the boundary of current LLM capabilities and motivate future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution. This diagnosis also clarifies why mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles, and why the geometric separation between instruction and execution pathways suggests limitations in neural introspection and mechanistic analysis.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Spurious Rewards Paradox: Mechanistically Understanding How RLVR Activates Memorization Shortcuts in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does spurious reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) activate memorization shortcuts in large language models, leading to improved accuracy on contaminated data despite incorrect rewards?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers an Anchor-Adapter circuit in Qwen models that explains how spurious RLVR triggers memorization shortcuts, leading to a Perplexity Paradox where answer perplexity decreases while prompt perplexity increases, and demonstrates causal steering via MLP interventions.
papers.conclusion: Our work demonstrates that reinforcement learning can inadvertently trigger shortcuts by activating latent memorized data rather than fostering genuine reasoning, providing tools to distinguish between appearance of capability and genuine generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Spurious RLVR leads to a Perplexity Paradox: answer token perplexity decreases while prompt perplexity increases, indicating memorization shortcuts.
A Functional Anchor in layers 18-20 triggers retrieval of memorized answers, while Structural Adapters in layers 21+ transform representations to accommodate the shortcut.
Neural Differential Equations show a bifurcation in the latent space trajectories between memorized and reasoned samples, with separation force peaking at the anchor layers.
Ablation studies confirm that the anchor layers are necessary for memorization on contaminated data, while stable reasoning remains unaffected.
Mechanistic intervention by scaling specific MLP keys allows bidirectional steering of the model's reliance on contaminated data.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is highly effective for enhancing LLM reasoning, yet recent evidence shows models like Qwen 2.5 achieve significant gains even with spurious or incorrect rewards. We investigate this phenomenon and identify a "Perplexity Paradox": spurious RLVR triggers a divergence where answer-token perplexity drops while prompt-side coherence degrades, suggesting the model is bypassing reasoning in favor of memorization. Using Path Patching, Logit Lens, JSD analysis, and Neural Differential Equations, we uncover a hidden Anchor-Adapter circuit that facilitates this shortcut. We localize a Functional Anchor in the middle layers (L18-20) that triggers the retrieval of memorized solutions, followed by Structural Adapters in later layers (L21+) that transform representations to accommodate the shortcut signal. Finally, we demonstrate that scaling specific MLP keys within this circuit allows for bidirectional causal steering-artificially amplifying or suppressing contamination-driven performance. Our results provide a mechanistic roadmap for identifying and mitigating data contamination in RLVR-tuned models. Code is available at https://github.com/idwts/How-RLVR-Activates-Memorization-Shortcuts.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Humanlike Cognitive Patterns as Emergent Phenomena in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of LLMs' emergent cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity, comparing them to human benchmarks and highlighting partial alignment, advancements in advanced models, and potential for collaboration.
papers.conclusion: The review synthesizes evidence that LLMs partially replicate human cognitive patterns, with notable advancements in reasoning and creativity, but limitations remain, indicating the need for further research in memory, attention, and open-source model development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate several human-like decision-making biases but lack others such as reflection effect and waste aversion.
Advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short.
LLMs show strong analogical reasoning abilities, sometimes surpassing human performance.
In creativity, LLMs excel in language-based tasks but struggle with divergent thinking requiring real-world context.
LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators to augment human creativity in problem-solving settings.
papers.limitation:
Over-reliance on GPT family models and insufficient testing of open-source LLMs, leading to potential bias and non-replication.
Memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs have not been sufficiently studied compared to decision-making, reasoning, and creativity.
future_direction: Study memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs
Increase testing and use of open-source LLMs
Adopt practices using multiple models in experiments
papers.abstract: Research on emergent patterns in Large Language Models (LLMs) has gained significant traction in both psychology and artificial intelligence, motivating the need for a comprehensive review that offers a synthesis of this complex landscape. In this article, we systematically review LLMs' capabilities across three important cognitive domains: decision-making biases, reasoning, and creativity. We use empirical studies drawing on established psychological tests and compare LLMs' performance to human benchmarks. On decision-making, our synthesis reveals that while LLMs demonstrate several human-like biases, some biases observed in humans are absent, indicating cognitive patterns that only partially align with human decision-making. On reasoning, advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short of human-level performance. A distinct dichotomy emerges in creativity: while LLMs excel in language-based creative tasks, such as storytelling, they struggle with divergent thinking tasks that require real-world context. Nonetheless, studies suggest that LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators, augmenting creativity in human-machine problem-solving settings. Discussing key limitations, we also offer guidance for future research in areas such as memory, attention, and open-source model development.

papers.title: Sculpting Large Language Models: Probing Structural Asymmetries in Layers and Embedding Spaces
papers.research_question: Whether large language models exhibit internal structural asymmetries and redundancies, and how such structure can be probed and leveraged for model optimization.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a sculpting methodology that reveals structural asymmetries in LLMs, showing that some layers and embedding dimensions are critical while others are redundant, providing insights for model optimization.
papers.conclusion: The findings challenge the notion of homogeneity in LLM components, suggesting they develop internal organization akin to biological or engineered systems, and outline future directions for leveraging this structure.
papers.key_findings:
The first transformer layer is disproportionately critical for model behavior.
Removal of the second half of layers (excluding the last) significantly impairs reasoning tasks.
Removing prime-indexed layers leads to selective degradation, suggesting internal specialization.
The second half of embedding dimensions can be zeroed with minimal performance loss, indicating redundancy.
Odd embedding dimensions are more semantically loaded than even ones, and some alterations (e.g., zeroing a single dimension) can occasionally improve performance, hinting at interference effects.
papers.limitation: The qualitative assessment of model responses (e.g., 'good', 'bad', 'crashed') and the limitations of llama.cpp's output format (e.g., inclusion of tags) constrain the analysis.
future_direction: Scaling up the sculpting approach to larger models (e.g., Mixtral, DeepSeek V3).
Benchmark refinement using granular and domain-specific tasks to uncover functional roles of components.
Exploring the structure of key-value caches to identify knowledge-specific subregions, inspired by DeepSeek V2's Memory Layer Attention (MLA).
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large Language Models (LLMs) are highly complex functions composed of massive parameters organized into layers and embedding dimensions. Yet, whether they exhibit internal structure—akin to biological systems or engineered constructs—remains poorly understood. In this work, we introduce a novel empirical approach to dissect LLM architectures through systematic ablation studies. Our experiments reveal that layers and embedding dimensions are not equal—some of them significantly influence model behavior, while others exhibit redundancy. These findings provide actionable insights for optimizing LLM efficiency and performance. We further propose a sculpting paradigm, wherein strategic modifications to model architecture to locate its internal structure to help to create new state-of-the-art models that both powerful and efficiency.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the language model perform multi-step reasoning by recalling memorized information or by following a step-by-step reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that language models perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning tree information can often be detected from attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that encode reasoning information degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with better accuracy and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The work considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
Analysis of multi-head attention is limited; shallow models with many heads might have different head functions.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that language models (LMs) have strong multi-step (i.e., procedural) reasoning capabilities. However, it is unclear whether LMs perform these tasks by cheating with answers memorized from pretraining corpus, or, via a multi-step reasoning mechanism. In this paper, we try to answer this question by exploring a mechanistic interpretation of LMs for multi-step reasoning tasks. Concretely, we hypothesize that the LM implicitly embeds a reasoning tree resembling the correct reasoning process within it. We test this hypothesis by introducing a new probing approach (called MechanisticProbe) that recovers the reasoning tree from the model's attention patterns. We use our probe to analyze two LMs: GPT-2 on a synthetic task (k-th smallest element), and LLaMA on two simple language-based reasoning tasks (ProofWriter & AI2 Reasoning Challenge). We show that MechanisticProbe is able to detect the information of the reasoning tree from the model's attentions for most examples, suggesting that the LM indeed is going through a process of multi-step reasoning within its architecture in many cases.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Large LSTMs trained on large datasets can represent syntactic state comparably to an explicitly syntactic model (RNNG), and data size is crucial for learning fine-grained lexical cues to syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: All models show basic incremental syntactic state representation, but capturing fine-grained lexical cues requires large amounts of data, while coarse-grained structure can be learned with either syntactic supervision or large data.
papers.key_findings:
All tested models show basic evidence of incremental syntactic state representation (e.g., subordinate clause licensing).
Only the large LSTMs (GRNN, JRNN) and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty).
All models show NP/Z garden path effects, but only large LSTMs are sensitive to verb transitivity as a cue.
All models show MV/RR garden path effects, but only large LSTMs and the RNNG are sensitive to verb morphology as a cue.
The representation of syntactic state degrades with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM).
future_direction: Using psycholinguistic methodology as a basis for more systematic tests of the linguistic competence of NLP systems.
papers.abstract: We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset; and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
