future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: Using Priming to Uncover the Organization of Syntactic Representations in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic representations organized in neural language models? Specifically, do LSTM language models track abstract syntactic properties such as the presence of a gap in relative clauses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel technique based on syntactic priming to analyze the organization of syntactic representations in neural language models. It finds that LSTM LMs' representations of sentences with relative clauses are organized hierarchically and track abstract properties like the presence of a gap.
papers.conclusion: The proposed priming technique reveals that LSTM language models organize syntactic representations in a linguistically interpretable manner, tracking abstract properties, though this ability diminishes with more training data.
papers.key_findings:
Sentences with the same syntactic structure are more similar to each other in the LM's representation space than lexically matched sentences with different structures.
Sentences with different types of relative clauses are more similar to each other than to sentences without relative clauses, suggesting LMs track the abstract property of having a gap.
LMs track linguistically interpretable features like reduction and passivity in relative clauses, with passivity contributing more to similarity than reduction.
For some linguistically interpretable classes, similarity between sentences is driven by more than just shared function words, indicating LMs track abstract properties.
The ability to track abstract properties decreases as the training corpus size increases.
papers.limitation:
For classes of sentences that do not share any function words (e.g., all relative clauses), the similarity between sentences in the LM's representation space may be driven purely by lexical items rather than abstract properties.
The hypothesis that similarity between object RCs and other RCs would predict agreement prediction accuracy was not supported.
future_direction: Explore how to bias models to track linguistically useful properties through architectural biases, training on auxiliary tasks, or data augmentation.
Generate a similarity matrix for human representations using priming experiments and compare with LM representations to gain insight into how human-like the LM representations are.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to syntactic structure. Drawing on the syntactic priming paradigm from psycholinguistics, we propose a novel technique to analyze the representations that enable such success. By establishing a gradient similarity metric between structures, this technique allows us to reconstruct the organization of the LMs' syntactic representational space. We use this technique to demonstrate that LSTM LMs' representations of different types of sentences with relative clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner, suggesting that the LMs track abstract properties of the sentence.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of\n Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models show evidence of incremental syntactic state representation, but the quality of representation depends on model architecture and training data size.
papers.conclusion: Psycholinguistic methods provide a valuable lens for probing the internal representations of neural language models, and representation of coarse-grained syntactic structure requires either syntactic supervision or large data, while exploiting fine-grained lexical cues requires large data.
papers.key_findings:
All models show basic evidence of syntactic state representation in subordinate clauses and garden path effects.
Large LSTMs (GRNN and JRNN) and the RNNG show more fine-grained sensitivity to syntactic cues, such as verb transitivity and morphological form.
Only GRNN and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty effect).
Large LSTMs use verb argument structure and morphological cues to modulate garden path effects, while TinyLSTM and RNNG do not.
Syntactic state representations degrade with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM) but not in others (JRNN and RNNG).
papers.abstract:
We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed
light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models
reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine
model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically
complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence
models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on
large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset;
and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that
the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans
of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the
small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Plug and Play Language Models: A Simple Approach to Controlled Text\n Generation
papers.research_question: How to control attributes of generated text (e.g., topic, sentiment) without modifying the model architecture or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for controlled text generation that combines a pre-trained language model with attribute classifiers without fine-tuning the LM, using gradients to steer generation.
papers.conclusion: PPLM is a simple, flexible approach to controlled text generation that does not require fine-tuning the LM and allows for combination of multiple attribute controllers.
papers.key_findings:
PPLM can control text generation for topics and sentiment using bag-of-words or simple classifiers.
It can detoxify text by following the negative gradient of a toxicity classifier.
It can combine multiple attributes during generation.
Evaluations show it achieves attribute alignment and fluency comparable to or better than baselines.
future_direction: Exploring more complex attribute models
Extending to other modalities
Improving the efficiency of the sampling process
papers.abstract:
Large transformer-based language models (LMs) trained on huge text corpora
have shown unparalleled generation capabilities. However, controlling
attributes of the generated language (e.g. switching topic or sentiment) is
difficult without modifying the model architecture or fine-tuning on
attribute-specific data and entailing the significant cost of retraining. We
propose a simple alternative: the Plug and Play Language Model (PPLM) for
controllable language generation, which combines a pretrained LM with one or
more simple attribute classifiers that guide text generation without any
further training of the LM. In the canonical scenario we present, the attribute
models are simple classifiers consisting of a user-specified bag of words or a
single learned layer with 100,000 times fewer parameters than the LM. Sampling
entails a forward and backward pass in which gradients from the attribute model
push the LM's hidden activations and thus guide the generation. Model samples
demonstrate control over a range of topics and sentiment styles, and extensive
automated and human annotated evaluations show attribute alignment and fluency.
PPLMs are flexible in that any combination of differentiable attribute models
may be used to steer text generation, which will allow for diverse and creative
applications beyond the examples given in this paper.

papers.title: Reward Models Identify Consistency, Not Causality
papers.research_question: Do reward models truly comprehend and reason about the questions they evaluate, or do they prioritize structural consistency over causal correctness?
papers.core_contribution: Reward models prioritize structural consistency and internal coherence of reasoning steps over causal understanding of the problem, raising concerns about their ability to evaluate true reasoning quality.
papers.conclusion: Current reward models have a consistency bias, evaluating logical structure rather than causal correctness, which necessitates a shift towards causality-aware reward models.
papers.key_findings:
Removing the problem statement (question truncation) has minimal impact on reward scores, indicating the question is not essential for evaluation.
Altering numerical values or disrupting the reasoning flow (e.g., truncating steps) significantly affects reward assignments, showing a reliance on structural consistency.
Reward models exhibit a strong dependence on complete reasoning trajectories; incomplete steps lead to significant variations in reward.
Reward models assess coherence rather than true reasoning quality, and the role of explicit problem comprehension is overstated.
Current reward models may be more effective at ranking responses than verifying logical validity.
future_direction: Causality-augmented training with counterfactual reasoning tasks.
Incorporating chain-of-thought awareness to reward logically structured reasoning chains.
Developing uncertainty-aware reward models and deeper reasoning signals.
papers.abstract: Reward models (RMs) play a crucial role in aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences and enhancing reasoning quality. Traditionally, RMs are trained to rank candidate outputs based on their correctness and coherence. However, in this work, we present several surprising findings that challenge common assumptions about RM behavior. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art reward models prioritize structural consistency over causal correctness. Specifically, removing the problem statement has minimal impact on reward scores, whereas altering numerical values or disrupting the reasoning flow significantly affects RM outputs. Furthermore, RMs exhibit a strong dependence on complete reasoning trajectories truncated or incomplete steps lead to significant variations in reward assignments, indicating that RMs primarily rely on learned reasoning patterns rather than explicit problem comprehension. These findings hold across multiple architectures, datasets, and tasks, leading to three key insights: (1) RMs primarily assess coherence rather than true reasoning quality; (2) The role of explicit problem comprehension in reward assignment is overstated; (3) Current RMs may be more effective at ranking responses than verifying logical validity. Our results suggest a fundamental limitation in existing reward modeling approaches, emphasizing the need for a shift toward causality-aware reward models that go beyond consistency-driven evaluation.

papers.title: Complexity Control Facilitates Reasoning-Based Compositional Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do complexity control strategies like initialization scale and weight decay influence transformers' ability to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Complexity control strategies, such as small initialization scales and large weight decay, enable transformers to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional tasks, leading to better out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.conclusion: Complexity control through initialization and weight decay is key to enabling transformers to learn compositional rules and generalize out-of-distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Models exhibit three phases based on initialization: poor generalization, good ID but poor OOD, and good ID and OOD generalization.
Complexity control (small init, large weight decay) promotes reasoning-based solutions with lower complexity bias.
Masking reveals that reasoning-based solutions use key token and anchor information differently.
Neuron condensation and structured embeddings are associated with reasoning phases.
Findings generalize to real-world tasks like image generation and NLP.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various tasks, yet their performance on compositional problems remains a subject of debate. In this study, we investigate the internal mechanisms underlying Transformers' behavior in compositional tasks. We find that complexity control strategies significantly influence whether the model learns primitive-level rules that generalize out-of-distribution (reasoning-based solutions) or relies solely on memorized mappings (memory-based solutions). By applying masking strategies to the model's information circuits and employing multiple complexity metrics, we reveal distinct internal working mechanisms associated with different solution types. Further analysis reveals that reasoning-based solutions exhibit a lower complexity bias, which aligns with the well-studied neuron condensation phenomenon. This lower complexity bias is hypothesized to be the key factor enabling these solutions to learn reasoning rules. We validate these conclusions across multiple real-world datasets, including image generation and natural language processing tasks, confirming the broad applicability of our findings.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Knowing Before Saying: LLM Representations Encode Information About Chain-of-Thought Success Before Completion
papers.research_question: Can the success of a zero-shot Chain-of-Thought process be predicted before completion, and do LLMs encode information about reasoning success in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal representations encode information about Chain-of-Thought success before generation, and a probing classifier can predict success, enabling potential early stopping.
papers.conclusion: The success of CoT reasoning can be predicted from LLM internal representations before generation, and these findings may inform methods to make CoT more efficient without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
A probing classifier based on LLM internal representations can predict CoT success before any token generation with 60% to 76.4% accuracy.
Internal representations outperform a BERT baseline that relies on generated tokens, indicating they encode deeper reasoning dynamics.
Providing later reasoning steps does not always improve prediction accuracy, and when it doesn't, earlier representations are more similar to later ones.
Early stopping experiments show that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.
The model's intermediate representations may encode sufficient information for correct answers, but zero-shot early stopping is suboptimal.
papers.limitation:
The test set for Mistral-7B was annotated by GPT-4o mini, which may be less reliable than human annotation, and results should be interpreted with caution.
Zero-shot early stopping is a suboptimal intervention because the model does not always converge to a stable answer even when nearly the entire reasoning sequence is generated.
future_direction: Using supervised learning to train the model to generate concise reasoning chains.
Using reinforcement learning to reinforce brevity via rewards.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether the success of a zeroshot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be predicted before completion.We discover that a probing classifier, based on LLM representations, performs well even before a single token is generated, suggesting that crucial information about the reasoning process is already present in the initial steps representations.In contrast, a strong BERT-based baseline, which relies solely on the generated tokens, performs worse-likely because it depends on shallow linguistic cues rather than deeper reasoning dynamics.Surprisingly, using later reasoning steps does not always improve classification.When additional context is unhelpful, earlier representations resemble later ones more, suggesting LLMs encode key information early.This implies reasoning can often stop early without loss.To test this, we conduct early stopping experiments, showing that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT at all, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.However, approaches like supervised learning or reinforcement learning designed to shorten CoT chains could leverage our classifier's guidance to identify when early stopping is effective.Our findings provide insights that may support such methods, helping to optimize CoT's efficiency while preserving its benefits.

papers.title: InTraVisTo: Inside Transformer Visualisation Tool
papers.research_question: How can we visualize and trace the internal computational processes of Transformer-based LLMs to understand their reasoning and errors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InTraVisTo, a tool that visualizes internal states and information flow in Transformer LLMs, and allows interactive embedding injection to probe model behavior.
papers.conclusion: InTraVisTo assists researchers in understanding and debugging LLMs, with future work aimed at improving decoding and integrating causal analysis.
papers.key_findings:
The tool visualizes the internal decoration process of transformers via decoded hidden states and information flow.
It can help identify specific layers where errors in generation occur, such as in a number reversal task.
Embedding injection allows users to modify internal states and observe the resulting changes in model output, enabling interactive probing.
future_direction: Better decoding and manipulation of hidden states, with particular attention on information injection.
Integration of causal analysis via mechanistic interpretability to better explain the 'causes' of a certain output.
papers.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have increased greatly over the last few years, as have their size and complexity. Nonetheless, the use of LLMs in production remains challenging due to their unpredictable nature and discrepancies that can exist between their desired behavior and their actual model output. In this paper, we introduce a new tool, InTraVisTo (Inside Transformer Visualisation Tool), designed to enable researchers to investigate and trace the computational process that generates each token in a Transformer-based LLM. InTraVisTo provides a visualization of both the internal state of the Transformer model (by decoding token embeddings at each layer of the model) and the information flow between the various components across the different layers of the model (using a Sankey diagram). With InTraVisTo, we aim to help researchers and practitioners better understand the computations being performed within the Transformer model and thus to shed some light on internal patterns and reasoning processes employed by LLMs.

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results. Our proposed approach enables the evaluation of more targeted hypotheses about the composition of meaning in the brain, expanding the range of possible scientific inferences a neuroscientist could make, and opens up new opportunities for cross-pollination between computational neuroscience and linguistics.

papers.title: Language Mixing in Reasoning Language Models: Patterns, Impact, and Internal Causes
papers.research_question: What are the patterns, performance impact, and internal causes of language mixing (reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt) in Reasoning Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of language mixing in Reasoning Language Models, showing it reflects latent internal processing preferences (a bias towards Latin and Han scripts) and that controlling the reasoning script via constrained decoding can significantly improve multilingual reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Language mixing in RLMs is a systematic behavior tied to the models' internal language preferences; controlling the reasoning script based on these preferences offers a practical way to optimize multilingual reasoning performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Language mixing is most prevalent when the input language is neither English nor Chinese, suggesting these serve as internal pivot languages.
The degree of language mixing increases with task difficulty and is more pronounced in STEM subjects.
Distillation amplifies language mixing compared to the base backbone models.
Forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy for non-Latin/Han-script input languages.
The script composition of reasoning traces closely mirrors that of the model's internal representations (analyzed via Logit Lens), indicating language mixing reflects latent processing preferences.
papers.limitation: Analysis focuses on valid reasoning traces that conclude with a final answer, excluding cases of endless reasoning.
future_direction: Controlling and adapting the reasoning language to build more robust, interpretable, and user-aligned RLMs.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models (RLMs) excel at complex tasks by leveraging a chain-of-thought process to generate structured intermediate steps. However, language mixing, i.e., reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt, has been observed in their outputs and shown to affect performance, though its impact remains debated. We present the first systematic study of language mixing in RLMs, examining its patterns, impact, and internal causes across 15 languages, 7 task difficulty levels, and 18 subject areas, and show how all three factors influence language mixing. Moreover, we demonstrate that the choice of reasoning language significantly affects performance: forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy. Finally, we show that the script composition of reasoning traces closely aligns with that of the model's internal representations, indicating that language mixing reflects latent processing preferences in RLMs. Our findings provide actionable insights for optimizing multilingual reasoning and open new directions for controlling reasoning languages to build more interpretable and adaptable RLMs.

papers.title: Improving Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can reasoning performance in LLMs be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning performance in LLMs can be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference, without any additional training.
papers.conclusion: The experiments indicate that reasoning can in part be understood to be encoded in the residual stream, similarly to how emotional valence or other features are encoded, and can be modulated via representation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Control vectors derived from contrastive pairs or PCA can improve model performance on inductive, deductive, and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The intervention generalizes across tasks: control vectors from bAbI improve GSM8K performance and vice versa.
The intervention changes the model's internal representations, as evidenced by changes in KL divergence and entropy.
The method requires no additional training and works by adding control vectors to the residual stream during inference.
The optimal scaling factor α varies across models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited scope of models (smaller than production-level state-of-the-art models).
The IOI task is relatively simple, which limits the scope of potential errors and the generalizability of findings.
The need for better contrastive pairs for reasoning to optimally derive control vectors.
future_direction: Applying the intervention to much larger models.
Applying the intervention to more general tasks.
Testing different contrastive schemes.
Exploring ways of embedding this methodology into the models.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have resulted in increasingly anthropomorphic language concerning the ability of LLMs to reason. Whether reasoning in LLMs should be understood to be inherently different is, however, widely debated. We propose utilizing a representation engineering approach wherein model activations are read from the residual stream of an LLM when processing a reasoning task. The activations are used to derive a control vector that is applied to the model as an inference-time intervention, modulating the representational space of the model, to improve performance on the specified task. We publish the code for deriving control vectors and analyzing model representations. The method allows us to improve performance on reasoning benchmarks and assess how control vectors influence the final logit distribution of a model via metrics such as KL divergence and entropy. We apply control vectors to Mistral-7B-Instruct and a range of Pythia models on an inductive, a deductive and mathematical reasoning task. We show that an LLM can, to a certain degree, be controlled to improve its perceived reasoning ability by modulating activations. The intervention is dependent upon the ability to reliably extract the model's typical state when correctly solving a task. Our results suggest that reasoning performance can be modulated in the same manner as other information-processing tasks performed by LLMs and demonstrate that we are capable of improving performance on specific tasks via a simple intervention on the residual stream with no additional training.

papers.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models (LLMs) reason via chain-of-thought prompting, and do they rely on simple heuristics rather than genuine reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the PRONTO QA dataset and uses formal analysis to show that LLMs are capable of correct individual deduction steps but struggle with proof planning when multiple valid steps are available.
papers.conclusion: While the largest LLMs are generally capable of reasoning, they have difficulty with proof planning and selecting the correct proof step when multiple options are available.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are capable of making valid individual proof steps, even in fictional contexts.
LLMs have difficulty with proof planning: when multiple valid proof steps are available, they often select the wrong step, leading to incomplete proofs.
Real-world knowledge helps reasoning: performance is significantly better with true ontologies compared to fictional or false ones.
Longer proofs (5 hops) are challenging, especially with top-down traversal of the ontology.
For larger models, the main source of error is misleading steps rather than invalid steps.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to modus ponens, proof lengths of at most 5, and semantically simple sentences.
future_direction: Use PRONTO QA to compare LLM reasoning with human reasoning and explore which aspects of human reasoning LLMs acquired.
Develop reasoning systems with more sophisticated proof planning/search strategies, such as neurosymbolic approaches.
Investigate whether LLMs can produce longer proofs, reason with other deduction rules, or handle more semantically complex sentences.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities given chain-of-thought prompts (examples with intermediate reasoning steps). Existing benchmarks measure reasoning ability indirectly, by evaluating accuracy on downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning. However, it is unclear how these models obtain the answers and whether they rely on simple heuristics rather than the generated chain-of-thought. To enable systematic exploration of the reasoning ability of LLMs, we present a new synthetic question-answering dataset called PrOntoQA, where each example is generated from a synthetic world model represented in first-order logic. This allows us to parse the generated chain-of-thought into symbolic proofs for formal analysis. Our analysis on InstructGPT and GPT-3 shows that LLMs are quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps, and so are generally capable of reasoning, even in fictional contexts. However, they have difficulty with proof planning: When multiple valid deduction steps are available, they are not able to systematically explore the different options.

papers.title: An explainable transformer circuit for compositional generalization
papers.research_question: How does a compact transformer achieve compositional induction? What is the underlying circuit responsible for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and mechanistically interprets the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer, and shows that this understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can implement structured and interpretable mechanisms for compositional functions, and disassembling transformer circuitry yields benefits for understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of specific attention heads that implement compositional induction, including Output Head, Primitive-Pairing Head, Question-Broadcast Head, RHS-Scanner Head, Primitive-Retrieval Head, and Function-Retrieval Head.
Validated the circuit through causal ablations, showing how index information flows from question to output.
Demonstrated that swapping positional embeddings in the circuit leads to predictable changes in attention patterns, confirming the causal role of the circuit.
Provided a program-like description of the algorithm implemented by the transformer circuit.
Showed that the circuit encodes both index-in-question and relative-index-on-LHS information, which are matched in the Output Head's QK alignment.
papers.limitation:
The circuit analysis focused on a relatively small transformer; it is unclear if similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
The techniques required substantial human effort (path-patching, ablations, interpretation); for large-scale models, manual approaches become less feasible.
Targeted activation swaps only partially perturb the model's behavior due to the distributed nature of the mechanism; complete perturbation requires coordinating interventions across multiple heads.
future_direction: Investigating whether similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
Developing automated or semi-automated methods for circuit discovery and interpretation to reduce human effort.
Creating systematic workflows for coordinating interventions across all heads to achieve complete perturbation.
papers.abstract: Compositional generalization-the systematic combination of known components into novel structures-remains a core challenge in cognitive science and machine learning. Although transformer-based large language models can exhibit strong performance on certain compositional tasks, the underlying mechanisms driving these abilities remain opaque, calling into question their interpretability. In this work, we identify and mechanistically interpret the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer. Using causal ablations, we validate the circuit and formalize its operation using a program-like description. We further demonstrate that this mechanistic understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably. Our findings advance the understanding of complex behaviors in transformers and highlight such insights can provide a direct pathway for model control.

papers.title: Composition, Attention, or Both?
papers.research_question: Whether the composition function and the self-attention mechanism can both induce human-like syntactic generalization in language models.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Composition Attention Grammars (CAGs), a novel architecture that combines a recursive composition function and a self-attention mechanism, and demonstrates that both components are important for inducing human-like syntactic generalization in language models.
papers.conclusion: The composition function and the self-attention mechanism both play an important role in making language models more human-like in their syntactic generalization, with the composition function specifically allowing syntactic features to percolate into subtree representations.
papers.key_findings:
CAGs achieved the highest overall accuracy on the SyntaxGym benchmark, outperforming even GPT-2 trained on 250x more data with a 7x larger model size.
Explicit syntactic supervision (+Syntax) consistently improved both overall accuracy and perplexity across model types.
The composition function (+Composition) improved syntactic generalization performance, suggesting it allows syntactic features (but not semantic features) to percolate into subtree representations.
The self-attention mechanism (+SelfAttn) improved performance only when combined with explicit syntactic supervision, highlighting the importance of attending to previous structural information, not just words.
A dissociation was observed between perplexity and human-like syntactic generalization performance among syntactic language models.
papers.limitation: CAGs have a high computational cost due to recursive training and the memory consumption of the self-attention mechanism, making it difficult to train larger models.
future_direction: Introduce a computationally efficient self-attention mechanism to CAGs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel architecture called Composition Attention Grammars (CAGs) that recursively compose subtrees into a single vector representation with a composition function, and selectively attend to previous structural information with a self-attention mechanism. We investigate whether these components—the composition function and the self-attention mechanism—can both induce human-like syntactic generalization. Specifically, we train language models (LMs) with and without these two components with the model sizes carefully controlled, and evaluate their syntactic generalization performance against six test circuits on the SyntaxGym benchmark. The results demonstrated that the composition function and the self-attention mechanism both play an important role to make LMs more human-like, and closer inspection of linguistic phenomenon implied that the composition function allowed syntactic features, but not semantic features, to percolate into subtree representations.

papers.title: A Survey on Large Language Models with some Insights on their Capabilities and Limitations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs generalize across diverse tasks, exhibit planning and reasoning abilities, and how can these emergent abilities be systematically elicited or enhanced? Also, what are the inherent limitations of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of LLMs, their capabilities, and limitations, with empirical insights into the Chain-of-Thought and Program-of-Thought abilities of Llama models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have transformative potential across diverse fields, but ethical, technical, and practical challenges remain, requiring continued research for responsible application.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit emergent abilities such as in-context learning, instruction following, and step-by-step reasoning.
The presence of code in pre-training data may contribute to the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LLMs can be used in various domains like healthcare, finance, education, and law.
Scaling laws play a crucial role in LLM performance.
LLMs have limitations including trade-offs associated with scaling and challenges in planning and reasoning.
papers.limitation: trade-offs associated with scaling
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly with the development of Large Language Models (LLMs) built on the transformer architecture, has redefined the capabilities of natural language processing. These models now exhibit remarkable performance across various language-related tasks, such as text generation, question answering, translation, and summarization, often rivaling human-like comprehension. More intriguingly, LLMs have demonstrated emergent abilities extending beyond their core functions, showing proficiency in tasks like commonsense reasoning, code generation, and arithmetic. This survey paper explores the foundational components, scaling mechanisms, and architectural strategies that drive these capabilities. Emphasizing models like GPT and LLaMA, we analyze the impact of exponential data and computational growth on LLM performance, while also addressing the trade-offs associated with scaling. We also examine LLM applications across sectors, such as healthcare, finance, education, and law, highlighting their adaptability and potential to solve domain-specific challenges. Central to this work are the questions of how LLMs generalize across diverse tasks, exhibit planning, and reasoning abilities, and whether these emergent abilities can be systematically elicited or enhanced. In particular, we provide some insights into the CoT (Chain of Thought) and PoT (Plan of Thought) abilities within LLMs, focusing on how pre-training data influences their emergence. Additionally, we investigate LLM-modulo frameworks that integrate external systems, allowing LLMs to handle complex, dynamic tasks. By analyzing these factors, this paper aims to foster the ongoing discussion on the capabilities and limits of LLMs, promoting their responsible development and application in novel and increasingly complex environments.

papers.title: Unlocking General Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Does long chain-of-thought reasoning represent a general capability encoded in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that long chain-of-thought reasoning is a general capability encoded in large language models, and introduces GLoRE, a training-free representation engineering method to effectively unlock this capability.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a deeper understanding of long CoT reasoning, paving the way for transparent and interpretable slow-thinking reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT representations are concentrated and distinct from vanilla CoTs, indicating a separate general capability encoded in LLMs.
Different domains share similar contrastive representations between long and vanilla CoTs, demonstrating transferability of long CoT reasoning.
Domain-specific information is required for effective long CoT reasoning, as representations in non-mathematical domains are more dispersed.
GLoRE outperforms all training-free baselines and even surpasses supervised fine-tuning in some scenarios while maintaining lower time complexity.
GLoRE is efficient, with the same time complexity as zero-shot CoT, as it injects representations without increasing input length or reasoning steps.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to the internal representations of the model, making it infeasible for closed-source LLMs.
Experiments are limited to representative tasks and LLMs due to constraints of cost and resources.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in long chain-of-thoughts(long CoTs) have significantly improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models(LLMs). Existing work finds that the capability of long CoT reasoning can be efficiently elicited by tuning on only a few examples and can easily transfer to other tasks. This motivates us to investigate whether long CoT reasoning is a general capability for LLMs. In this work, we conduct an empirical analysis for this question from the perspective of representation. We find that LLMs do encode long CoT reasoning as a general capability, with a clear distinction from vanilla CoTs. Furthermore, domain-specific representations are also required for the effective transfer of long CoT reasoning. Inspired by these findings, we propose GLoRE, a novel representation engineering method to unleash the general long CoT reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of GLoRE in both in-domain and cross-domain scenarios.

papers.title: Circuit Compositions: Exploring Modular Structures in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural networks implement reusable functions through subnetworks that can be composed to perform more complex tasks? Specifically, how do circuits for functionally related tasks relate to each other in terms of node overlap and cross-task faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation pruning through continuous sparsification to automatically discover faithful and minimal circuits for sequence-to-sequence tasks, analyzes the modularity of circuits for functionally related string-edit operations, and demonstrates that circuits can be composed via set operations to represent more complex functions.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a method for circuit discovery and shows that circuits for compositional tasks exhibit modularity and can be composed, providing insights into the modular structure of transformer-based language models.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits identified by activation pruning are both faithful and minimal.
Functionally similar circuits exhibit notable node overlap and cross-task faithfulness.
Circuits can be combined through set operations (e.g., union) to create subnetworks that perform more complex tasks.
papers.limitation:
The method does not guarantee completeness of circuits.
The identified circuits depend on the ablation paradigm (mean vs. zero ablation).
Findings are based on a small model and controlled dataset, and may not generalize to larger models and more complex tasks.
future_direction: Explore more efficient ways to quantify completeness and incorporate it into the optimization framework.
Scale the findings to larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Unveiling Internal Reasoning Modes in LLMs: A Deep Dive into Latent Reasoning vs. Factual Shortcuts with Attribute Rate Ratio
papers.research_question: How do latent reasoning and factual shortcuts differ during inference in LLMs for multi-hop questions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) metric to efficiently distinguish between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts in LLMs, and provides an analysis of internal mechanisms showing that latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate steps.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically investigates distinctions between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts, proposes the ARR metric for efficient classification, and demonstrates its application in RAG conflict scenarios, deepening understanding of model reasoning pathways.
papers.key_findings:
Subject representations differ significantly between reasoning modes: latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information for final answer extraction, while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate reasoning and resemble single-hop factual queries.
The proposed Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) achieves around 90% accuracy in classifying reasoning modes on constructed datasets.
Model behavior under conflicting prompts in RAG scenarios is closely tied to its underlying reasoning mode, with latent reasoning more influenced by external context and factual shortcuts more robust to disruptive information.
The model undergoes two disjointed stages during multi-hop reasoning: local shallow reasoning (encoding relation-related attributes) and deep reasoning (integrating information for final answer).
Bridge-related information propagated from the subject position plays a decisive role in second-hop reasoning for latent reasoning modes.
papers.limitation:
Scope limited to two-hop reasoning, which may not generalize to more complex reasoning chains.
Limited dataset availability for studying latent reasoning due to many shortcut mappings in training data.
Latent multi-hop reasoning pathway identification relies on CoT filtering, which may not fully correspond to the model's internal reasoning processes.
The proposed metric lacks rigorous verification due to model complexity and limited datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex reasoning beyond two-hop tasks.
Further refinement and verification of the ARR metric.
Investigating the balance between external information utilization and robustness in RAG conflicts.
papers.abstract: Yiran Yang, Haifeng Sun, Jingyu Wang, Qi Qi, Zirui Zhuang, Huazheng Wang, Pengfei Ren, Jing Wang, Jianxin Liao. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Wave to Syntax: Probing spoken language models for syntax
papers.research_question: Do spoken language models encode syntactic structure, and how does it vary across layers, model sizes, and training objectives?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that spoken language models encode syntactic structure, with encoding strongest in middle layers and enhanced by model size and specific training objectives.
papers.conclusion: The results confirm that spoken language models encode a moderate level of syntactic information, with encoding affected by training objectives and model size.
papers.key_findings:
Syntax is encoded in spoken language models, but weaker than in text-based models like BERT.
Syntax encoding is most prominent in the middle layers of the networks.
Larger model size is associated with stronger encoding of syntactic information.
Fine-tuning for ASR improves syntax encoding compared to pre-training only.
Self-supervised objectives lead to a dip in syntax encoding in final layers, while visually-supervised objectives do not.
papers.limitation:
The study only looks at sentence-level representations.
Only English datasets are used.
future_direction: Extend experiments to sub-sentence level probing
Compare syntax encoding across different languages
papers.abstract: Understanding which information is encoded in deep models of spoken and written language has been the focus of much research in recent years, as it is crucial for debugging and improving these architectures. Most previous work has focused on probing for speaker characteristics, acoustic and phonological information in models of spoken language, and for syntactic information in models of written language. Here we focus on the encoding of syntax in several self-supervised and visually grounded models of spoken language. We employ two complementary probing methods, combined with baselines and reference representations to quantify the degree to which syntactic structure is encoded in the activations of the target models. We show that syntax is captured most prominently in the middle layers of the networks, and more explicitly within models with more parameters.

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: Self-conditioning pre-trained language models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained Transformer-based Language Models (TLMs) control text generation, and can internal expert units be identified and activated to condition generation without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to condition pre-trained language models by identifying and activating internal expert units (neurons) without fine-tuning or extra parameters, enabling control over fine-grained concepts and bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The self-conditioning method is effective for controlling text generation in pre-trained TLMs without fine-tuning, provides insights into their internal generative mechanisms, and can be used for applications like bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Activating a surprisingly small number of expert units (as few as 3 in a 345M parameter model) is sufficient to steer text generation towards a desired concept.
The method achieves gender parity in generated text with lower perplexity compared to FUDGE and PPLM-BoW.
The conditioning strength (number of units to intervene on) required to achieve parity correlates with the model's intrinsic bias for a given context.
The method can successfully condition on fine-grained homograph concepts, distinguishing between different word senses.
The intervention exploits a natural generative mechanism within the TLM and does not require fine-tuning or additional parameters.
papers.limitation:
Requires a set of positive and negative example sentences for each concept, which might be costly to collect for some concepts.
Intervening on too many expert units can degrade the fluency and linguistic correctness of the generated text.
future_direction: Automatically selecting the number of expert units (k) to intervene on based on the model's unconditional bias for a context.
Extending the method to other modalities or model architectures.
Investigating the interplay between different concepts and their corresponding expert units.
papers.abstract: In this paper we aim to investigate the mechanisms that guide text generation with pre-trained Transformer-based Language Models (TLMs). Grounded on the Product of Experts formulation by Hinton (1999), we describe a generative mechanism that exploits expert units which naturally exist in TLMs. Such units are responsible for detecting concepts in the input and conditioning text generation on such concepts. We describe how to identify expert units and how to activate them during inference in order to induce any desired concept in the generated output. We find that the activation of a surprisingly small amount of units is sufficient to steer text generation (as little as 3 units in a model with 345M parameters). While the objective of this work is to learn more about how TLMs work, we show that our method is effective for conditioning without fine-tuning or using extra parameters, even on fine-grained homograph concepts.
